For the mantle geometry, I'm weighing a lathe-based bulbous egg shape versus a scaled sphere primitive, settling on dimensions around 0.35m tall and 0.25m wide, positioned slightly back and up so the funnel sits forward beneath it, with the arms resting flat on the floor and curling at their tips for the rest pose.

The degenerate segment at the axis should produce zero-area triangles, which is fine for rendering. Now I need to figure out sizing: setting the mantle height to roughly 0.3m with the lathe anchored at its base, scaling the profile points accordingly so the overall octopus proportions feel right compared to arm span. I'm considering whether the eyes deserve their own joints -- giving each a hinge-style joint could make the rig more expressive even though eyes don't strictly need them, so I'll add "eyeL" and "eyeR" joints parented to the mantle for that extra rigging value. Next I'm thinking about the funnel/siphon as a small cone-like protrusion under the front of the mantle, angled forward and down.

For the eight arms, I'm picturing each as a chain extending radially from a central hub on the underside, lying flat with curling tips, using sweep geometry with tapering radius to give that classic tentacle shape.

For suckers, I'm thinking small discs placed along the inner side of each arm, and for the pale belly coloring I'll use a sector-based paint to differentiate the dorsal clock from the underside arc. For overall skin styling, I'm leaning toward a reddish-orange mottled look with pale spots to capture that classic octopus coloring in a stylized way.

Given octopus arms spread radially with tips curling upward, I'll put the suckers along the ventral band around 180 degrees, accepting that most will be hidden against the floor but visible where the arms curl off the ground.

With 8 arms and roughly 14 suckers each, I'm looking at over 100 small parts total, which stays well within mesh and triangle limits if I keep each sucker as a single simple shape sharing a few materials. I'll model each sucker as a small torus to mimic the ring-like look of a real sucker rather than building multi-layer discs.

Working through the torus orientation and positioning math so the rings sit flush against the arm surface without penetrating too deeply, I'm weighing whether it's worth the complexity versus just using a painted spot pattern on the arms to fake the sucker look instead.

Now I'm laying out the arms themselves: 8 of them radiating from the hub underside at staggered angles, tapering from a thick base near the mantle down to thin curled tips, with lengths around 0.45 and varying cross-sections so they don't overlap the hub awkwardly.
